links.claim: The implementation record explains the boundary this way: See XLS-85 and xrpl.js flag 17. No mainnet support is claimed. - The writer receives the principal only by publishing K through a successful finish. A relay can submit the same fulfillment; funds still go to the original destination. Buyer cancellation is policy-only and cannot win before expiry. - K becomes public. This is acceptable because each ciphertext is encrypted for one buyer and intent with a fresh key; it does not unlock other buyers' copies. It is not DRM: anyone with that ciphertext and public K can read that copy. - A writer can commit to nonsense or an undecryptable envelope and collect. The cryptographic proof establishes responsibility, not truth or automatic damages. Existing challenges/reputation handle broken promises; this is not a truth oracle. - K may appear in an unvalidated submitted finish. The buyer still waits for validation. Ledger outages/history gaps retain reservations pending reconciliation. - A dishonest buyer can create extra escrow objects outside policy. This product guarantees one charge per policy intent, not control of arbitrary wallet activity. - Conditional finish costs more than a Payment. The XRPL fee formula scales as base_fee × (33 + fulfillment_bytes / 16) before multisign/load effects. Here K is 32 bytes and its encoded fulfillment is 36 bytes. At the observed 12-drop signing base, ceil(12 × (33 + 36/16)) = 423 drops. A 2,000-drop cap rejects excessive fees. Live create/cancel each cost 12 drops. A cancelled 60,000-drop principal is fully returned; its buyer still pays 24 drops in fees. - Synthetic corpus and extractive fixture answers in the proof are labelled; Testnet value transfer is real Testnet execution, with no real value. For a reader assessing this result, the operative distinction is between a documented mechanism and a freshly verified transaction. Reproduction requires checking the actual receipt and its ledger evidence, rather than treating this note as a live network probe.
